title: Lab: where does the energy go?
summary: Split a workload's energy into data movement and arithmetic and see why on-chip reuse matters.

blocks.md: Energy follows the same split as time: $E \approx D_{vol} E_{move} + O\,E_{op}$. The coefficients used in this lab are illustrative orders of magnitude: about 100 pJ per byte from DRAM, about 10 pJ per byte from on-chip SRAM, and about 1 pJ for a 16-bit multiply-add. The exact values depend on the chip; the ratio is what drives design.

blocks.title: Try it: DRAM against on-chip reuse

challenge.md: The workload moves 1 TB and performs 10¹³ operations. Serve the bytes from **on-chip SRAM** (10 pJ/byte) instead of DRAM. What is the total energy in joules?
challenge.explanation: 10 J for movement plus 10 J for compute = 20 J, down from 110 J with DRAM. Same arithmetic, 5.5x less energy.

assert abs(energy_j(1e12, 10, 1e13, 1) - 20) < 1e-9

blocks.hint: pJ are 10⁻¹² J: `(bytes_moved * pj_per_byte + ops * pj_per_op) * 1e-12`.

questions.q: With DRAM at 100 pJ/byte, what percentage of the lab workload's energy is data movement (whole number)?
Which design change attacks the largest energy term here?
options: Keeping operands on chip and reusing them (tiling, systolic arrays)
questions.explanation: Reuse cuts the bytes fetched from DRAM; that is the motivation behind tiling, systolic arrays and operator fusion.

points: E ≈ bytes × energy per byte + ops × energy per op.
An off-chip byte costs on the order of 100x a 16-bit multiply-add.
On-chip reuse saves energy as well as time.
